title: NVIDIA DGX H100
summary: The 8xH100 reference training node: 640 GB HBM3, NVLink fabric, ~32 PFLOPS FP8.
details: The DGX H100 packs eight H100 SXM GPUs (80 GB HBM3 each) with NVLink/NVSwitch giving 900 GB/s GPU-to-GPU bandwidth, plus dual CPUs and 2 TB system memory. It delivers about 32 petaFLOPS of FP8 tensor compute per node and is the building block of H100 clusters (DGX SuperPOD scales to thousands). For planners, one DGX H100 is the unit of capacity: training math is usually quoted in 'DGX-days' or 'H100-hours'.

demo.title: DGX-H100 capacity math
demo.program:
gpus, fp8_per_gpu = 8, 4e15  # ~4 PFLOPS FP8 dense per H100
print(f"node FP8: {gpus*fp8_per_gpu/1e15:.0f} PFLOPS")
print(f"HBM3: {8*80} GB; NVLink: 900 GB/s all-to-all")

title: NVIDIA DGX H200
summary: DGX H100's successor node: 8xH200 with 141 GB HBM3e each — 1.1 TB of GPU memory per node.
details: The DGX H200 keeps the 8-GPU DGX form factor but upgrades each GPU to 141 GB of HBM3e (1.1 TB per node) with 4.8 TB/s memory bandwidth per GPU. The extra memory directly extends maximum model size and context length per node before tensor parallelism must span nodes. Compute is similar-class to H100; the win is memory capacity for long-context and large-model training.

demo.title: H200 vs H100 memory
demo.program:
for name, mem in [("H100", 80), ("H200", 141)]:
    print(f"{name}: {8*mem} GB/node; 70B fp16 needs {140/(8*mem):.1%} of node")

title: NVLink / NVSwitch
summary: NVIDIA's GPU-to-GPU fabric: 900 GB/s per GPU on H100 systems — the fast lane inside the node.
details: NVLink connects GPUs directly at 900 GB/s bidirectional per H100 (4th gen), and NVSwitch fabrics let all 8 GPUs in a node talk all-to-all at full speed. This is what makes tensor parallelism practical: sharded layers exchange activations every step without touching the slower network. Between nodes, traffic moves to InfiniBand or Ethernet — the NVLink domain ends at the node boundary, which is why parallelism strategies are designed around it.
capacity: 900 GB/s per GPU (NVLink 4.0); 7.2 TB/s bisection per node
cost_notes: Included in DGX/node price; NVL72 extends domain to rack

demo.title: All-reduce time on NVLink
demo.program:
size_gb, bw_gbs = 80, 900  # one H100's gradients
# ring all-reduce ~ 2*(n-1)/n * size / bw
t = 2 * 7/8 * size_gb / bw_gbs
print(f"80GB all-reduce over NVLink: {t*1000:.0f} ms")

title: InfiniBand NDR
summary: 400 Gb/s per port fabric for inter-node training traffic — the standard for large GPU clusters.
details: InfiniBand NDR runs 400 Gb/s per port (with 800 Gb/s XDR arriving), with RDMA and adaptive routing that keep all-reduce collectives fast across thousands of GPUs. NCCL is tuned for it, and 'rail-optimized' topologies give each GPU a dedicated rail to its peers. For clusters above ~64 GPUs, InfiniBand (or high-end RoCE Ethernet) is effectively mandatory — training throughput collapses on oversubscribed networks.

demo.title: Inter-node all-reduce estimate
demo.program:
size_gb, bw_gbs, gpus = 80, 50, 256  # 400Gb/s = 50 GB/s
t = 2 * (gpus-1)/gpus * size_gb / bw_gbs
print(f"80GB all-reduce, 256 GPUs, NDR: {t:.1f} s")

title: AWS EC2 P5 Instances
summary: AWS's 8xH100 cloud instances with EFA networking — on-demand H100s without buying hardware.
details: EC2 P5 instances provide 8 H100 GPUs, 3.2 Tb/s EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) networking, and up to 3200 Gbps aggregate network bandwidth per instance. P5en adds newer networking; P6 (B200) is the next step. Pricing is on-demand (~$100+/hr per instance), reserved, or spot — spot P5 can be 60-70% cheaper but preemptible. HyperPod adds Slurm-managed cluster orchestration for multi-hundred-GPU runs.
capacity: 8x H100 per instance; scales to 1000s via HyperPod
cost_notes: ~$98/hr on-demand per p5.48xlarge; spot much cheaper

demo.title: Launch a P5 spot fleet (AWS CLI)
demo.program:
aws ec2 request-spot-instances \
  --instance-type p5.48xlarge \
  --spot-price "30.00" \
  --launch-specification '{"ImageId":"ami-0abc","KeyName":"train-key"}'

title: Google Cloud A3 Instances
summary: GCP's 8xH100 VMs with GPUDirect-TCPX — Google's on-ramp to H100 training.
details: GCE A3 VMs offer 8 H100 80GB GPUs with NVIDIA GPUDirect-TCPX networking for efficient multi-node collectives, plus local NVMe. A3 Mega doubles the network bandwidth for large runs. Google pairs them with GKE for Kubernetes-native training or managed Vertex AI Training. Committed-use discounts cut ~40% off on-demand for steady workloads.
capacity: 8x H100 per VM; A3 Mega for large runs

demo.title: Committed-use savings

title: Azure ND H100 v5
summary: Azure's 8xH100 VMs on InfiniBand NDR — Microsoft's flagship training SKU.
details: Azure ND H100 v5 VMs pack 8 H100s with 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NDR per GPU via 8 ConnectX-7 NICs — one of the strongest per-GPU network ratios in the cloud. They underpin Azure's OpenAI supercomputing partnership and are available in NDv5 clusters for large runs. Azure ML provides the managed training layer; low-priority/spot VMs offer deep discounts for fault-tolerant workloads.

demo.title: Per-GPU network ratio
demo.program:
print("NDv5: 400 Gb/s per GPU =", 400/8, "Gb/s per H100 vs")
print("typical: 200-400 Gb/s shared per node")

title: Lambda Labs GPU Cloud
summary: Developer-friendly H100/A100 cloud with simple pricing — popular with startups and researchers.
details: Lambda Labs offers on-demand and reserved H100, H200, A100, and GH200 instances with straightforward hourly pricing and no hyperscaler complexity. Their 1-click clusters provide multi-node setups with InfiniBand-class networking. Pricing has historically undercut the big three clouds, making Lambda a favorite for fine-tuning and mid-size training runs.

demo.title: SSH to a Lambda instance
demo.program:
ssh ubuntu@<instance-ip>
nvidia-smi  # verify 8x H100
# then: torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py

title: CoreWeave
summary: The GPU-specialist cloud: Kubernetes-native H100/H200 capacity built for AI labs.
details: CoreWeave built a cloud purpose-designed for GPU workloads — bare-metal Kubernetes, InfiniBand fabrics, and large H100/H200/GB200 reservations. They power runs for labs like Mistral and scale to tens of thousands of GPUs. Their model is capacity-first: reserve fleets of the newest GPUs with SUNK-style SLAs, aimed at serious training rather than casual inference.
cost_notes: Reserved contracts; premium vs spot markets

demo.title: Fleet cost sketch
demo.program:
gpus, per_gpu_hr, days = 1024, 3.5, 30
print(f"1024 GPUs x 30d @ ${per_gpu_hr}/hr = ${gpus*per_gpu_hr*24*days:,.0f}")

title: Together AI GPU Clusters
summary: Research-friendly GPU cloud from the RedPajama team — good for open-model training.
details: Together AI (the team behind RedPajama) offers GPU clusters aimed at researchers and open-model builders, with H100/A100 capacity and tooling tuned for training and serving open weights. Their pricing and researcher programs made them a hub for the open LLM community's training runs.

demo.title: Run-cost comparison

title: Vast.ai Marketplace
summary: Peer-to-peer GPU rentals: bid on spare GPUs worldwide, often the cheapest per-hour price.
details: Vast.ai is a marketplace where hosts rent spare GPUs — from RTX 3090s to H100s — and renters bid. Prices are frequently the lowest available (a fraction of on-demand cloud), but instances are interruptible, heterogeneous, and vary in network quality. Best for fault-tolerant fine-tuning and inference; large tightly-coupled training needs care in host selection.
interconnect: Varies by host (check before NCCL runs)

demo.title: Search Vast.ai for cheap 4090s
demo.program: vastai search offers 'gpu_name=RTX_4090 num_gpus=2' --order 'dph_total' | head -20

title: RunPod
summary: Instant GPU pods for development and fine-tuning — fast spin-up, template ecosystem.
details: RunPod rents GPU pods by the second with a template ecosystem (PyTorch, Stable Diffusion, vLLM one-clicks). Secure Cloud is their managed tier; Community Cloud is cheaper peer capacity. It is optimized for getting a GPU in under a minute — ideal for fine-tuning experiments and inference endpoints rather than month-long pretraining.

demo.title: Fine-tune cost on RunPod
demo.program:
rate, hours, runs = 0.69, 6, 20  # 4090 secure cloud example
print(f"{runs} runs x {hours}h @ ${rate}/hr = ${rate*hours*runs:.0f}")

title: FLOPs Budgeting
summary: The 6*N*D rule: estimate any training run's compute before spending a dollar.
details: FLOPs budgeting uses the approximation that training a transformer costs ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token (forward + backward). Multiply by hardware throughput at realistic MFU (30-50%) to get GPU-hours, then dollars. This single formula sizes everything from fine-tunes to frontier runs and is the first calculation in any serious training plan.

demo.title: Budget a 7B run on 2T tokens
demo.program:
params, tokens = 7e9, 2e12
flops = 6 * params * tokens
h100 = 989e12 * 0.45  # BF16 peak x 45% MFU
hrs = flops / h100 / 3600
print(f"{flops:.2e} FLOPs -> {hrs:,.0f} H100-hours (~${hrs*3:,.0f} @ $3/hr)")

title: Chinchilla Scaling Laws
summary: DeepMind's finding: most models are undertrained — scale data and parameters equally.
details: The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed that for compute-optimal training, parameters and training tokens should scale in equal proportions (~20 tokens per parameter), and that many famous models were dramatically undertrained. Chinchilla (70B on 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B) at equal compute. The laws now guide every data-vs-size decision; practitioners still often overtrain small models deliberately for cheaper inference (the 'inference-optimal' trade-off).
cost_notes: Overtraining small models trades train cost for inference savings

demo.title: Chinchilla-optimal tokens
demo.program:
for p in [7e9, 70e9, 405e9]:
    print(f"{p/1e9:.0f}B params -> {p*20/1e12:.1f}T tokens optimal")

title: Spot / Preemptible GPUs
summary: Use interruptible capacity at 60-90% discounts — with checkpointing to survive eviction.
details: Spot (AWS), preemptible (GCP), and low-priority (Azure) GPUs sell spare capacity at deep discounts but can be reclaimed with minutes of notice. Training on spot requires frequent checkpointing, elastic worker counts, and restart-tolerant launchers — standard practice now via frameworks that handle preemption. Savings of 60-90% make spot the default for cost-sensitive fine-tuning.

demo.title: Spot savings
demo.program:
ondemand, spot, hrs = 8.0, 2.0, 1000
print(f"on-demand: ${ondemand*hrs:,.0f} vs spot: ${spot*hrs:,.0f} "
      f"(save ${ondemand*hrs-spot*hrs:,.0f})")

title: Slurm
summary: The HPC workload manager that schedules most academic and lab GPU clusters.
details: Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) allocates nodes, queues jobs, and enforces fair-share policies on GPU clusters. Training scripts launch via sbatch with #SBATCH directives requesting GPUs, memory, and time; squeue/scancel manage the queue. Nearly every university and many industry clusters run Slurm — knowing sbatch is table stakes for cluster training.

demo.title: Submit a training job to Slurm
demo.program:
sbatch <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4 --gpus-per-node=8 --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
srun torchrun --nnodes=4 train.py
EOF

title: Kubernetes GPU Scheduling
summary: Run training on K8s with GPU operators, gang scheduling, and elastic scaling.
details: Kubernetes with the NVIDIA GPU Operator, device plugins, and gang schedulers (Volcano, Kueue) brings cloud-native orchestration to training: containerized jobs, elastic scaling, and multi-tenancy. CoreWeave and hyperscalers run GPU fleets on K8s. The trade-off vs Slurm is complexity — K8s shines at mixed training+inference platforms, Slurm at pure HPC throughput.

demo.title: Gang-scheduling check
demo.program:
job = {"gpus": 32, "min_available": 32}
print("gang-schedulable:" , job["gpus"] >= job["min_available"])

title: High-Throughput Storage (WEKA)
summary: Training thousands of GPUs needs storage that feeds them — WEKA, VAST, and parallel file systems.
details: GPU clusters stall without fast storage: checkpointing terabytes and streaming datasets to thousands of workers needs 100s of GB/s. WEKA, VAST Data, and Lustre/BeeGFS parallel file systems provide POSIX or S3-speed access at scale. Sizing rule: aggregate read bandwidth should keep dataloaders ahead of the GPUs, and checkpoint writes should finish in minutes, not hours.
cost_notes: Major capex line; cloud: FSx/EFS variants

demo.title: Checkpoint write time
demo.program:
ckpt_gb, bw_gbs = 2000, 100  # 2TB checkpoint, 100 GB/s
print(f"checkpoint write: {ckpt_gb/bw_gbs/60:.0f} min; "
      f"hourly ckpts cost {ckpt_gb/bw_gbs:.0f}s of training each")

title: Data Center Power Planning
summary: A DGX H100 draws ~10 kW; a thousand-GPU cluster is a power plant problem.
details: Power is the hidden constraint: a DGX H100 rack draws ~10 kW, and a 10,000-GPU cluster needs tens of megawatts plus cooling (often liquid). Power planning covers utility feeds, PUE (power usage effectiveness), backup, and increasingly, direct power-purchase agreements. Many cluster projects are gated more by megawatts than by GPU purchase orders.

demo.title: Cluster power draw
demo.program:
nodes, kw_per_node, pue = 128, 10, 1.3
mw = nodes * kw_per_node * pue / 1000
print(f"{nodes} nodes: {mw:.1f} MW (PUE {pue})")

title: GPU Failure Rates
summary: At thousand-GPU scale, something is always broken — plan checkpointing and spares accordingly.
details: Large runs see constant hardware churn: Meta reported hundreds of GPU failures during LLaMA-3 training. Best practice: N+ spare nodes, health checks before job start (node problem detectors), checkpoint every 30-60 minutes, and automatic restart from the last good checkpoint. Mean time between failures for a 10K-GPU run can be hours — resilience engineering is part of training engineering.

demo.title: Expected failures per run
demo.program:
gpus, mtbf_gpu_h, run_h = 10000, 200000, 720  # 30-day run
expected = gpus * run_h / mtbf_gpu_h
print(f"expected GPU failures in run: {expected:.0f}")

title: RoCE vs InfiniBand
summary: RDMA over Converged Ethernet: cheaper than InfiniBand, catching up with Ultra Ethernet.
details: RoCE runs RDMA over Ethernet, reusing cheaper Ethernet switches at the cost of trickier congestion control. InfiniBand has historically won on raw collective performance, but hyperscalers (AWS EFA, Google) bet on Ethernet variants, and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium is standardizing AI-optimized Ethernet. For new clusters, the choice is cost (RoCE/Ethernet) versus turnkey performance (InfiniBand).
cost_notes: Ethernet switches cheaper per port than IB

demo.title: Fabric cost comparison

title: MFU Metrics
summary: Model FLOPs Utilization: the honest measure of how well your cluster is actually training.
details: MFU = achieved FLOPs/sec divided by hardware peak. Well-tuned LLM training hits 40-55% MFU on H100s; below 30% signals dataloader, communication, or kernel problems. Paired with HFU (hardware FLOPs utilization, including recomputation), MFU is the KPI of training efficiency work — every optimization (FlashAttention, better overlap, packing) shows up here first.
cost_notes: Each MFU point = real dollars at scale

demo.title: MFU from a training log
demo.program:
achieved_tflops, peak_tflops = 420, 989
mfu = achieved_tflops / peak_tflops
print(f"MFU: {mfu:.1%}")

title: NCCL Collectives
summary: NVIDIA's communication library: the all-reduce engine under every multi-GPU run.
details: NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) implements all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast, and point-to-point optimized for NVLink and InfiniBand, with topology detection and ring/tree algorithms chosen automatically. Every distributed training framework (PyTorch DDP/FSDP, DeepSpeed) calls NCCL under the hood. Tuning NCCL (channels, IB vs SHM transports) is a standard step in cluster bring-up.

demo.title: Test NCCL bandwidth
demo.program:
# nccl-tests all_reduce_perf across nodes:
/opt/nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 8G -f 2 -g 8

title: TCO Modeling
summary: Total cost of ownership: GPUs are only ~half the cost of a cluster.
details: TCO models add GPUs, networking, storage, power, cooling, facilities, staff, and 3-5 year refresh to get true cost per GPU-hour. Networking and power often surprise first-time builders at 30-40% of capex. Cloud-vs-build decisions hinge on utilization: sustained >60% utilization favors building; bursty research favors cloud.
cost_notes: Rule: utilization decides build vs cloud

demo.title: Build vs cloud breakeven
demo.program:
build_per_gpu_hr, cloud_per_gpu_hr = 1.8, 3.5
for util in [0.3, 0.6, 0.9]:
    build = build_per_gpu_hr / util
    print(f"util {util:.0%}: build ${build:.2f}/eff-hr vs cloud ${cloud_per_gpu_hr:.2f}")

title: Per-Token Cost Estimation
summary: Translate training and inference into dollars per million tokens for budgeting.
details: Per-token math connects training FLOPs to money: training cost per token = 6*N*D dollars-per-FLOP; inference cost per token follows from model size, hardware, and batching. Teams budget features ('this agent costs $0.02 per task') and compare providers on $/M tokens. It is the unit economics language of applied AI.
cost_notes: Inference: ~$0.15-15 per M tokens by model size

demo.title: Inference cost per 1M tokens
demo.program:
params, flops_per_token = 70e9, 2*70e9
h100_hr, tflops = 3.0, 989e12*0.4
tps = tflops / flops_per_token
cost_per_m = h100_hr / 3600 / tps * 1e6
print(f"70B rough cost: ${cost_per_m:.2f}/M tokens")
